landing_meta_title: RCOS Compass — Consent-based governance for communities
landing_meta_description: Turn the open RCOS standard into a short list of what your ecovillage, cohousing or land trust still has to decide — then discuss, consent and keep a clear record of every decision.
landing_meta_audience: Ecovillages, intentional communities, cohousing, land trusts, farm collectives and groups still forming
landing_meta_image_alt: The RCOS Compass logo and the words: Find your way to agreements everyone can live with.
landing_hero_badge: Community governance, built on the open RCOS standard
landing_hero_lede: RCOS Compass guides your community from the first open question to a written, shareable rulebook — through real conversation, consent and a clear record of what you decided and why.
landing_hero_audience: For ecovillages, cohousing, land trusts — and groups still looking for their land.

landing_tour_path_title: What Valle Verde still has to decide
landing_tour_path_sub: 23 open questions, ordered so each answer makes the next one easier.
landing_tour_lena_says: When Pablo left, it took eight months to settle his share. I never want us to do that to anyone again.
landing_tour_marco_says: Agreed. The standard asks us to settle shared assets before anyone leaves — we only ever wrote down the notice. I’ll draft something.
landing_tour_lint_clean: The linter has nothing left to flag
landing_tour_ready_to_freeze: No objections after Tomás’s concern was folded into v3. A steward can record this version as a decision.

landing_story_title: From “who decided that?” to rules everyone can find.
landing_story_lede: Valle Verde is 27 people on fourteen hectares of hillside. They share a kitchen, a well and plenty of opinions. Scroll through their first year with Compass.
landing_story_s1: The greenhouse went up on a Tuesday. Half the group had agreed in the kitchen; the other half found out from the greenhouse. Nobody was wrong. There was just nowhere to look it up.
landing_story_s2: Ana uploads the 2019 bylaws, three years of meeting notes and the house rules — PDF, Word, OpenDocument, Markdown or plain text. Compass reads them passage by passage. Nothing gets thrown away.
landing_story_s3: Each passage is matched to the part of the RCOS standard it answers, and a member confirms every match. Quiet hours? Covered. Leaving the community? Half-written. Conflict? Never discussed — and now everyone can see it, calmly, before it matters.
landing_story_s4: The Path turns 23 open questions into an order that makes sense. The stewards choose the priority — unblock the most, close the riskiest gaps, or build on what’s working — and Compass does the sorting.
landing_story_s5: Lena opens a discussion on what happens to someone’s things when they leave. It’s linked to the exact part of the standard it answers, so everyone knows what’s actually being asked.
landing_story_s6_title: Propose — with a friendly second reader.
landing_story_s6: Marco drafts a proposal. The linter notices that “as soon as possible” can’t be checked by anyone and asks him to say by when. It’s still his rule — he writes 90 days.
landing_story_s7: Members consent, abstain or object. Tomás objects — with a reason. The proposal is amended, and the round goes on until nobody has a reason to block it.
landing_story_s8: The version everyone can live with becomes a decision — with who was present, why, and when to look at it again. It’s DEC-2026-015 now, findable for good.
landing_story_s9: One register holds every decision, its version and the people who made it. “Who decided the greenhouse?” now takes about four seconds.
landing_story_s10: Before a tense meeting, Sofía types how the group handles dominant speakers. Compass shows the clauses and decisions that govern it, with their references — and says plainly what Valle Verde hasn’t decided yet. It points to the rule; it never answers for the group.
landing_story_s11: Decisions carry a review date, and Compass reminds you when one comes up. When a rule stops fitting, take it back to its discussion and freeze a new version. The old decision stays on record, marked as replaced.
landing_story_s12: Decisions assemble into real documents. Export the Exit & Separation Protocol as a PDF or as Markdown, or publish it to a public page for the land trust, the bank — or the next person who asks to join.
landing_story_s13_title: Always know how far you’ve come.
landing_story_s13: A live view shows members how much of the standard you’ve covered, layer by layer — and which gaps would hurt most if a conflict started tomorrow.
landing_story_s14: Tap any term — consent, steward, provisional — for a plain explanation. The glossary and the standard are built in, and when the standard falls short you can say so, right where you noticed.

landing_features_title: The questions every community ends up asking.
landing_features_lede: Compass is built around them — not around meetings, files or tools.
landing_f_consent_text: Consent, abstain or object — with reasons. Objections improve proposals instead of ending them.

landing_rcos_title: A checklist of everything a community eventually has to decide.
landing_rcos_lede_before: RCOS — the Regenerative Community Operating System — is an open standard for community governance, free to use under CC BY 4.0. It doesn’t tell you
landing_rcos_lede_after: to decide — it makes sure you don’t forget to decide it. Seven layers, from who you are to how your rules can change.
landing_rcos_p1: Leaving, money and conflict are where communities split. RCOS puts them on the table early.
landing_rcos_p2_title: Works with how you already decide
landing_rcos_p2: Consensus, sociocracy, majority vote — the standard asks that you choose, not which.
landing_rcos_p3: Free to use, written in plain language, and improved by the communities who use it.
landing_rcos_modules: Modules: extra standards for particular kinds of community, tracked alongside RCOS-Core rather than added to it.

landing_layer_6_text: How any of this can change.
